title: Report types and custom report types
objectives: Explain that a report type is the template that decides which records and fields a report can use.
Contrast Salesforce-provided report types with custom report types you define in Setup.
Choose 'must have related records' versus 'may or may not have related records' for a custom report type relationship.
Treat a custom report type as metadata and the rows a report returns as business data.
diagnostic_question: A manager wants Opportunities with Products plus a custom child object that no standard report type includes. Would you clone a standard report type, build a custom report type, or invent a joined report first—and what relationship setting would you pick?
definition: A report type is the template that determines which records and fields appear in a report. Salesforce ships standard report types; a custom report type lets an admin define a primary object and related objects, then choose whether each parent must have related children or may appear with or without them. ([Choose a Report Type](https://help.salesforce.com/s/articleView?id=sf.reports_builder_editing.htm); [Custom Report Types](https://help.salesforce.com/s/articleView?id=xcloud.reports_report_type_setup.htm))
why_it_matters: The wrong report type is the most common reason a field is 'missing' from the builder or a parent row disappears. Interviewers listen for inner versus outer related-object semantics, not for clicking New Report. Custom report types are metadata with edition allocations; reports run against live records.
sixty_second_explanation: Think of a report type as a restaurant tasting menu: it lists which courses (objects) and ingredients (fields) a diner can order together. A standard menu is printed by the restaurant. A custom report type is a chef-designed tasting menu that joins a primary course to related courses. 'Must have related records' is a set menu that drops anyone who skipped the side dish. 'May or may not have related records' keeps the diner even if the side dish never arrived.
deeper_explanation: When you create a report, the first choice is a report type. Salesforce Help states that the report type you choose determines which records and fields appear. The Opportunities report type, for example, exposes Opportunity records and fields such as Amount, Stage, and Type. ([Build a Report in Salesforce Classic](https://help.salesforce.com/s/articleView?id=sf.reports_builder_editing.htm))

Standard report types come with the platform and with many features. Service Help notes that some custom report types appear only after you enable a related feature, such as Cases with Historical Trending when historical trend reporting is on. ([Use Custom Report Types to Report on Support Activity](https://help.salesforce.com/s/articleView?id=service.reports_support_crts.htm))

A custom report type is created in Setup. You pick a primary object and related objects, then set each relationship to require related records or to allow parents with or without children. Help documents that when the relationship is 'A records may or may not have related B records,' filters on the child may not exclude the parent the way users expect. ([Custom Report Types](https://help.salesforce.com/s/articleView?id=xcloud.reports_report_type_setup.htm))

Custom report types count against an org allocation regardless of development status. Salesforce Help lists 50 for Professional, 300 for Enterprise, 2,000 for Unlimited and Performance, and 400 for Developer Edition. ([Reports and Dashboards Limits and Allocations](https://help.salesforce.com/s/articleView?id=analytics.rd_reports_dashboards_limits.htm))

The custom report type definition is metadata. Running a report reads business records. Changing the report type's field layout or object relationships changes which columns later reports can use; it does not insert Opportunities.

mental_model.analogy: A tasting menu at a restaurant: the menu (report type) decides which courses can be ordered together; the plates that actually arrive are the records.
useful_mapping: standard report type → printed house menu
custom report type → chef-designed tasting menu in Setup
related object → later course on the same ticket
must have related records → diner is dropped if the side dish is missing
may or may not have related records → diner stays even without the side dish
field layout on the report type → ingredients listed as orderable
report rows → plates that arrived tonight (business data)
where_it_breaks: A restaurant does not enforce field-level security; Salesforce still hides fields the running user cannot see.
Menus do not have edition allocations; custom report types do.
Joined reports (ANA-002) can combine multiple report types in blocks—this lesson is the menu, not the newspaper layout.
The analogy does not encode the 2,000-row display cap (ANA-005).

teach_back_prompt: Explain standard versus custom report types to a sales manager using the tasting-menu analogy, then name one place the analogy breaks and when you would choose 'must have related records.'

review_schedule.prompt: From memory: what does a report type decide, and how does a custom report type differ from a standard one?
Given four requests (missing field, missing child object, parents without children, too many CRTs), pick report type vs custom report type vs another tool.
Draw the tasting-menu mapping and state where inner versus outer related-object semantics break user expectations on child filters.
Walk a 'field not in the builder' ticket from report type field layout to FLS without opening notes.
Two-minute interview: custom report types as metadata, allocations, and one relationship-setting trap.

interview_explanation.thirty_seconds: A report type is the template for which objects and fields a report can use. Standard types ship with Salesforce. Custom report types add relationships you design. 'Must have related' drops parents without children; 'with or without' keeps them.
interview_explanation.two_minutes: I start from the question: which objects must appear together. If a standard report type already includes them, I use it. If a custom object or lookup is missing, I create a custom report type in Setup—that is metadata with an edition allocation. I then pick must-have versus with-or-without related records, because an outer relationship can leave parent rows on the report even when child filters look like they should hide them. Fields still have to be on the report type and visible by FLS. The report type is not the same as a joined report, which stitches multiple types into blocks.

terminology.plain: The template that decides which objects, records, and fields a report can use.
terminology.precise: Salesforce Help: the report type you choose determines which records and fields appear in your report.
terminology.example: Choosing Opportunities so Amount, Stage, and Type are available in the builder.
terminology.non_example: A saved report named 'Q4 Pipeline' is an instance that uses a report type; it is not itself the type.
terminology.confusable_neighbor: Report format (tabular, summary, matrix, joined) — layout of the same type's data, covered in ANA-002.
terminology.boundary: This lesson owns the template. Formats, filters, and dashboards are later ANA topics.

terminology.plain: A report type Salesforce already provides for common object combinations.
terminology.precise: Platform- or feature-shipped report types. Some appear only after a related feature is enabled.
terminology.example: Opportunities, or Cases with Historical Trending after historical trending is enabled.
terminology.non_example: A report type an admin built in Setup for Account plus a custom LAB_ child object.
terminology.confusable_neighbor: Custom report type: admin-defined in Setup.
terminology.boundary: Do not assume every standard type exists in every org; feature flags matter.

terminology.plain: An admin-defined report type that joins a primary object to related objects you choose.
terminology.precise: A Setup metadata definition. Counts against the org's custom report type allocation regardless of development status.
terminology.example: LAB_Account with LAB_Site_Visit__c as a related object so field staff can report both.
terminology.non_example: Adding a column to an existing Opportunities report does not create a custom report type.
terminology.confusable_neighbor: Joined report: multiple report types in blocks, not a new type definition.
terminology.boundary: Allocations are in the Reports and Dashboards limits table; do not invent extra editions.

terminology.plain: The first object on a custom report type—the 'A' in A-with-B.
terminology.precise: The driving object for the report type's relationship chain. Related objects hang off this object.
terminology.example: Account as primary, with Contacts as the related object.
terminology.non_example: A dashboard running user is not a primary object.
terminology.confusable_neighbor: Report's first grouping field: a display choice, not the report type's primary object.
terminology.boundary: Maximum relationship depth is not quoted here without a fetched Help sentence.

terminology.plain: Only parent rows that have at least one related child appear.
terminology.precise: Inner-style relationship: each A record must have at least one related B record.
terminology.example: Accounts that actually have Opportunities, dropping Accounts with none.
terminology.non_example: A field filter for Amount greater than 0 is not this relationship setting.
terminology.confusable_neighbor: Cross filter WITH (ANA-003): a report-level related-object filter, not the report type definition.
terminology.boundary: Changing this setting changes which rows every report of that type can see.

terminology.plain: Parent rows appear even if they have no related children.
terminology.precise: Help documents this as 'A records may or may not have related B records.' Child filters may not exclude those parents as users expect.
terminology.example: All Accounts, with Opportunity columns blank when no Opportunity exists.
terminology.non_example: Exporting a report to Excel is not a relationship setting.
terminology.boundary: Interviewers often ask why 'filter on child = empty' still shows parents—start here.

terminology.plain: The list of fields the custom report type makes available to the report builder.
terminology.precise: Fields not included on the custom report type cannot be added as columns, even if they exist on the object.
terminology.example: Adding LAB_Priority__c to the CRT layout so builders can column it.
terminology.non_example: Page layout and compact layout control record pages, not report types.
terminology.confusable_neighbor: Field-level security: even a laid-out field is hidden if the user lacks FLS.
terminology.boundary: Needs verification of exact Lightning CRT editor labels in the target org.

terminology.plain: Whether the custom report type is still being built or is available for general report creation.
terminology.precise: Limits Help counts custom report types regardless of development status. UI labels such as In Development versus Deployed should be verified in-org.
terminology.example: Leaving a new CRT in development so only admins trial it before wider use.
terminology.non_example: Apex class API version is unrelated.
terminology.confusable_neighbor: Report folder visibility: who can run a saved report, not CRT status.
terminology.boundary: Exact permission names for who can see in-development CRTs: Needs verification in current Help.

when_to_use: When a standard report type does not include a custom object, lookup, or field combination the report must show.
When interviewers ask why a field is missing from the report builder: start with the report type, then FLS.
When you must choose must-have versus with-or-without related records so parent rows appear or disappear correctly.
When you are counting custom report types against Professional, Enterprise, Unlimited, Performance, or Developer allocations.
when_not_to_use: Do not create a custom report type merely to change grouping layout; that is tabular, summary, matrix, or joined format (ANA-002).
Do not use a custom report type as a substitute for a dashboard, subscription, or dynamic running user (ANA-004).
Do not expect a custom report type to bypass sharing, FLS, or the 2,000-row display cap (ANA-005).
Do not build a custom report type when CRM Analytics datasets or Tableau extracts are the actual requirement (ANA-006).
configuration_or_code_location: Setup → Report Types (custom report type metadata).
Reports tab → New Report → choose a report type.
Object Manager is for object/field definition, not for report type relationships.
Limits: Reports and Dashboards Limits and Allocations in Salesforce Help.

worked_example.scenario: A sandbox lab needs a report of LAB_Account rows with optional LAB_Site_Visit__c children. Standard report types do not include the custom child. Leadership also wants a second report of only accounts that actually have a visit.
inputs: Synthetic data only; no production accounts

decisions.decision: Create a custom report type rather than forcing a joined report first.
decisions.because: The gap is a missing related object on one type, not two unrelated types side by side.
decisions.rejected: Joined report with empty second block as a workaround

decisions.decision: Build one CRT with 'may or may not have related' visits for the full account list.
decisions.because: That relationship keeps accounts with zero visits.
decisions.rejected: Must-have related records for the 'all accounts' report

decisions.decision: Use a second CRT or a must-have relationship for 'accounts that have visits.'
decisions.because: Inner-style related records drop parents without children at the type layer.
decisions.rejected: Relying only on a child Amount filter on an outer CRT, which Help warns may not exclude parents as expected

configuration_or_code: Setup → Report Types → New Custom Report Type: LAB_Account with LAB_Site_Visit__c.
Set relationship to with-or-without for the coverage report; must-have for the visits-only report (or a second type).
Add LAB_ fields to the CRT field layout; run both reports against synthetic rows.
worked_example.output: Coverage report lists every LAB_Account; visits-only report lists only accounts with at least one LAB_Site_Visit__c.
verification: An account with zero visits appears on the with-or-without report and not on the must-have report.
A field omitted from the CRT layout cannot be added as a column.
Setup still shows the new custom report types counting toward the org allocation.
worked_example.self_explanation: The report type, not a later filter, decided whether childless parents existed. I treated CRT definitions as metadata and used only LAB_ records.

hands_on_lab.environment: Disposable Developer sandbox or Trailhead Playground; synthetic LAB_ objects or standard Account/Contact only.
starting_state_checks: You can create custom report types.
steps: Create a custom report type with Account as primary and Contact as related, using may-or-may-not-have related records.
Build a report of that type and confirm an Account with no Contacts still appears.
Clone or edit a second type (or relationship) to must-have related Contacts and confirm childless Accounts disappear.
Remove one Contact field from the CRT layout and confirm it vanishes from the builder.
guided_completion: If childless Accounts still appear on the must-have type, the relationship is not inner.
If a field is missing, check CRT layout before FLS.
hands_on_lab.independent_challenge: Document one standard Service custom report type that appears only after a feature is enabled, using Salesforce Help, without enabling it in production.
evidence: Screenshot of both reports' row counts with LAB_ or synthetic names only.
One sentence: report type is metadata; rows are data.
stop_recovery_cleanup: Delete lab custom report types and lab reports from the sandbox.
Do not deploy unused CRTs to production.
hands_on_lab.limitations: This lab does not prove joined-report blocks, dashboard running user, or sharing.

decision_table.signal: The Create Report list already includes the objects and fields the business named.
decision_table.choose: Use the existing standard or custom report type as-is.
decision_table.not: A brand-new custom report type that duplicates Opportunities plus Account.
decision_table.why: The report type already determines those records and fields; extra CRTs consume allocation.

decision_table.signal: A custom object or lookup never appears on any standard report type.
decision_table.choose: Create a custom report type with that primary and related object.
decision_table.not: Export to Excel as the long-term reporting design.
decision_table.why: Custom report types exist to define object relationships the shipped types omit.

decision_table.signal: Leadership wants every parent row, including those with zero children.
decision_table.choose: Custom report type relationship 'may or may not have related' children.
decision_table.not: Must-have related records, which drops childless parents.
decision_table.why: Outer-style related records keep parents; inner-style does not.

decision_table.signal: Leadership wants only parents that actually have a child row.
decision_table.choose: Must-have related records on the custom report type (or an equivalent inner type).
decision_table.not: A child-field filter on a with-or-without type, hoping parents vanish.
decision_table.why: Help warns child filters on may-or-may-not types may not exclude parents as expected.

decision_table.signal: A field exists on the object but not in the report builder for this type.
decision_table.choose: Add the field to the custom report type layout, then recheck FLS.
decision_table.not: Assume Salesforce 'lost' the field or that a page layout controls reports.
decision_table.why: The report type decides available fields; page layouts do not.

limitations: Does not teach cross filters or report formulas (ANA-003).
Custom report type allocations are edition-specific and counted even in development.
Feature-gated types appear only after the related feature is enabled.
security_notes: A report type does not grant record access; sharing and FLS still apply at run time.
Putting a sensitive field on a CRT layout makes it available to anyone who can build reports of that type and who has FLS.
Use synthetic LAB_ data in examples; never paste real customer rows into handbook notes.
common_mistakes: Calling a saved report a report type.
Using a custom report type when a standard type already fits.
Choosing with-or-without and then blaming 'bad filters' for childless parents.
Looking at page layout instead of CRT field layout for a missing column.
Ignoring that CRT counts include in-development types.

troubleshooting.symptom: A field on the object does not appear in the report builder.
check: Is the field on this report type (standard coverage or CRT layout)?
Does the running user have field-level security to read it?
troubleshooting.do_not_assume: The field is missing from the object.

troubleshooting.symptom: Parent records with no children are missing (or unexpectedly present).
check: Custom report type relationship: must-have versus may-or-may-not.
Whether the user is looking at a different saved report that uses another type.
troubleshooting.do_not_assume: Sharing deleted the parents; the type may have inner-joined them out.

troubleshooting.symptom: Cannot create another custom report type.
check: Edition allocation in Reports and Dashboards Limits Help.
troubleshooting.do_not_assume: The org 'lost' the Report Types menu.

production_notes: Create and trial custom report types in a sandbox; they are metadata.
Document inner versus outer related-object choice in the CRT description.
Watch allocations before cloning CRTs per team.
This lesson does not authorize production experiments on live customer reports.

mcqs.prompt: According to Salesforce Help, what does the report type you choose determine?

options.A: Which records and fields appear in the report
options.C: Only whether the report is tabular or matrix
options.D: Only the org's custom report type allocation

mcqs.rationale: Help states the report type determines which records and fields appear.

distractor_explanations.B: Running user is a dashboard concern (ANA-004).
distractor_explanations.C: Format is chosen after the type (ANA-002).
distractor_explanations.D: Allocation is a limit on how many CRTs you may define, not what one report shows.

mcqs.prompt: Where do you define a custom report type?

options.A: Setup as metadata relating a primary object to related objects

mcqs.rationale: Custom report types are Setup-defined templates for reporting relationships.

distractor_explanations.B: Page layouts do not define report types.
distractor_explanations.C: Flow is automation, not a report type.
distractor_explanations.D: CRM Analytics datasets are a different product (ANA-006).

mcqs.prompt: Do in-development custom report types count toward the org allocation?

options.A: Yes. Limits apply to all custom report types regardless of development status
options.C: Only if they have been used in a dashboard

mcqs.rationale: The allocations table states limits apply regardless of development status.

distractor_explanations.B: Status does not exempt the count.
distractor_explanations.C: Dashboard use is irrelevant to the CRT count.
distractor_explanations.D: The regardless-of-status rule is not PE-only.

mcqs.prompt: Enterprise Edition custom report type allocation listed in Help is:
mcqs.rationale: Help lists 300 for Enterprise, 50 Professional, 2,000 Unlimited/Performance.

distractor_explanations.D: 5 is dashboard filters per dashboard, not CRTs.

mcqs.prompt: A field exists on Opportunity but does not appear when building a report. What should you check first among these?

options.A: Whether the chosen report type includes that field
options.B: Whether the dashboard has a dynamic running user
options.C: Whether Apex sharing recalculation ran this hour
options.D: Whether the report format is joined

mcqs.rationale: The report type determines available fields; format and dashboards come later.

distractor_explanations.B: Dashboards consume reports; they do not add object fields to a type.
distractor_explanations.C: Sharing affects which rows appear, not which columns exist in the builder.
distractor_explanations.D: Joined format still uses report types per block.

mcqs.prompt: You need every Account, including those with no Opportunities. Which custom report type relationship matches?

options.A: Accounts may or may not have related Opportunities
options.B: Each Account must have at least one Opportunity
options.C: A joined report is the only option

mcqs.rationale: With-or-without related records keeps parents that have zero children.

distractor_explanations.B: Must-have drops Accounts with no Opportunities.
distractor_explanations.C: Joined reports combine types; they are not required for this relationship.
distractor_explanations.D: Tabular is a format, not a report type relationship.

mcqs.prompt: Why might Cases with Historical Trending be missing from Create Report?

options.A: The related feature is not enabled, so that custom report type has not appeared
options.D: Custom report types cannot include Case

mcqs.rationale: Service Help: some CRTs become available only when related features are enabled.

distractor_explanations.B: Joined reports are a format, not this enablement gate.
distractor_explanations.C: Format is independent of type availability.
distractor_explanations.D: Case has many support report types.

mcqs.prompt: Users filter a with-or-without CRT report on a child field and still see parents. Likely cause?

options.A: May-or-may-not related records can leave parent rows even when child filters look exclusive
options.B: The report type allocation was exceeded
options.C: Dashboards cannot use custom report types
options.D: All reports cap at five custom report types

mcqs.rationale: Help documents unexpected parent rows when the CRT uses may-or-may-not related B records.

distractor_explanations.B: Allocation blocks creating types, not filter semantics.
distractor_explanations.C: Dashboards can use reports built on CRTs.
distractor_explanations.D: There is no five-CRT-per-report rule in the cited limits.

mcqs.prompt: A developer says 'just add the field to the page layout so it shows on reports.' What is wrong?

options.A: Report columns come from the report type (and FLS), not from the page layout
options.B: Page layouts are the only way to add report columns
options.D: Fields on page layouts automatically become dashboard widgets

mcqs.rationale: The report type determines fields; page layouts control record pages.

distractor_explanations.D: Widgets consume reports, not page layouts.

mcqs.prompt: Unlimited Edition needs many custom report types. Help lists which allocation?
mcqs.rationale: Unlimited and Performance: 2,000 CRTs in the allocations table.

mcqs.prompt: Custom report type versus joined report?

options.A: A CRT defines one type's object graph; a joined report places multiple report types in blocks
options.C: Joined reports replace the need for any report type
options.D: A CRT is only for dashboards

mcqs.rationale: This lesson owns the type template; joined format is ANA-002.

distractor_explanations.C: Every joined block still uses a report type.
distractor_explanations.D: CRTs are used by reports, which dashboards may then consume.

mcqs.prompt: Custom report type metadata versus the rows a user sees?

options.A: The CRT definition is configuration metadata; running the report reads business records
options.B: Creating a CRT inserts one dummy record per object
options.C: Report rows are stored inside the CRT metadata file
options.D: Deleting a CRT deletes all related business records

mcqs.rationale: Types are Setup metadata; reports query live (or sandbox) data.

distractor_explanations.B: No dummy insert is part of CRT create.
distractor_explanations.C: Rows are queried at run time.
distractor_explanations.D: Deleting metadata does not mass-delete those objects' records.

flashcards.back: Which records and fields appear in reports that use that type.
Standard types ship with Salesforce or a feature. Custom report types are defined in Setup.

flashcards.front: When do you create a custom report type?
flashcards.back: When no existing type includes the objects, lookups, or fields the report must use.
Only parent records that have at least one related child are included.

flashcards.front: May or may not have related records means?
flashcards.back: Parents appear even with zero children; child filters may not drop those parents as users expect.

flashcards.front: Enterprise Edition custom report type allocation?

flashcards.back: 2,000 custom report types regardless of development status.

flashcards.front: Professional Edition custom report type allocation?
Field on the object but not in the builder?
flashcards.back: Check whether the report type includes the field, then field-level security.

flashcards.front: Does a page layout control report columns?
flashcards.back: No. The report type (and FLS) does. Page layouts control record pages.

flashcards.front: Is a custom report type the same as a joined report?
flashcards.back: No. A CRT is one type's object graph. Joined reports put multiple types in blocks.
Enable the related feature; some CRTs appear only then.
The type definition is metadata. Report output is queried records.

flashcards.front: Need parents with zero children on the report?
flashcards.back: Use with-or-without related records, not must-have.

flashcards.front: Does a report type bypass sharing?
flashcards.back: No. Sharing and FLS still apply when the report runs.

flashcards.front: Developer Edition custom report type allocation?
flashcards.back: 400 custom report types per the limits table.

interview_questions.question: What is a report type, and how is a custom report type different?
interview_questions.answer_30_seconds: A report type is the template for which records and fields a report can use. Standard types ship with Salesforce. A custom report type is Setup metadata that relates a primary object to related objects you choose.
interview_questions.answer_2_minutes: I treat the report type as the first design choice, before format or filters. If Opportunities already has the fields, I use the standard type. If a custom child object is missing, I create a custom report type: primary object, related objects, then must-have versus with-or-without children. That definition is metadata and counts toward an edition allocation even while in development. Running the report still reads live records through sharing and FLS.
interview_questions.example: LAB_Account plus LAB_Site_Visit__c cannot use a standard Opportunities type, so the admin creates a CRT.
tradeoffs: Reuse a standard type vs consume CRT allocation
Inner related records vs keeping childless parents
follow_ups: What is the Enterprise CRT allocation?
How is this different from a joined report?
weak_answer_warnings: Calling the saved report the report type
Saying page layouts add report columns

interview_questions.question: Why would a field exist on an object but not in the report builder?
interview_questions.answer_30_seconds: The chosen report type does not include that field, or the running user lacks FLS. Page layouts do not control report columns.
interview_questions.answer_2_minutes: I check the report type first because Help says the type determines records and fields. On a custom report type I inspect the field layout. Then I check FLS for the user who will run it. I do not start with dashboard running user or Apex. If the field is on another object not related on this type, the fix is a new or extended custom report type, not a formula hack on the wrong type.
interview_questions.example: LAB_Priority__c is on the custom object but was never added to the CRT layout, so builders cannot column it.
tradeoffs: Add the field to an existing CRT vs create another type
follow_ups: What if the object itself is missing from Create Report?
weak_answer_warnings: Telling them to add the field to the page layout

interview_questions.question: Sales wants all Accounts, including those with no Opportunities. How do you set the custom report type?
interview_questions.answer_30_seconds: Use a custom report type where Accounts may or may not have related Opportunities so childless parents remain on the report.
interview_questions.answer_2_minutes: Must-have related Opportunities would drop Accounts with none, which fails the requirement. With-or-without keeps those parents. I warn that filters on Opportunity fields may not remove those parents the way users expect; if they later want only Accounts that have deals, I switch to must-have or a second type rather than piling child filters on an outer CRT. I still confirm FLS and sharing so they are not mixing 'no Opportunity' with 'Opportunity I cannot see.'
interview_questions.example: Coverage report of every LAB_Account, Opportunity columns blank when no child exists.
tradeoffs: One outer CRT vs two types
Blank child columns vs a cleaner inner report
follow_ups: What happens if they filter Amount greater than zero on the outer type?
Would a cross filter be better later?
weak_answer_warnings: Saying joined report is the only answer

interview_questions.question: A stakeholder asks you to 'just clone Opportunities' into a custom report type for every team. How do you respond?
interview_questions.answer_30_seconds: I refuse duplicate CRTs that match a standard type. Custom report types consume edition allocation even in development, and they add maintenance.
interview_questions.answer_2_minutes: I ask what field or related object the standard Opportunities type lacks. If nothing is missing, we use the standard type and control access with folders (ANA-004). If each team truly needs a different related object, I still look for one well-named CRT rather than a clone per region. I cite the limits table: Enterprise 300, Unlimited 2,000, and development status does not hide the count. Cloning for folder politics is the wrong tool.
interview_questions.example: Three regions want the same Opportunity plus Account fields; one standard type plus three folders beats three identical CRTs.
follow_ups: What is the Professional Edition cap?
Do deleted CRTs free allocation immediately? Needs verification.

interview_questions.question: Users say Accounts vanished after you 'fixed' the custom report type. What do you check?
interview_questions.answer_30_seconds: I check whether the relationship changed to must-have related children, which drops parents with zero children. Then I confirm they are on the same report type.
interview_questions.answer_2_minutes: A switch from with-or-without to must-have is an inner join at the type layer: Accounts without Opportunities disappear from every report of that type. I compare row counts in a sandbox with a known childless LAB_Account. I also verify they did not switch saved reports. Sharing is a later check (ANA-005) if the type still includes those parents for an admin. I do not start with dashboard subscriptions.
interview_questions.example: Childless LAB_Account present yesterday, gone after CRT relationship edit to must-have Opportunities.
tradeoffs: Fix the type vs create a second type for coverage
Communicate the semantic change vs silent edit
follow_ups: How would FLS hide Opportunity Amount but not the Account?
Does this affect dashboards sourced from those reports?

interview_questions.question: Create Report does not list Cases with Historical Trending. What else might be true?
interview_questions.answer_30_seconds: That custom report type may appear only after historical trend reporting is enabled for Cases. Feature-gated types are documented in Service Help.
interview_questions.answer_2_minutes: I do not immediately build a duplicate CRT. I check whether the related feature is on, because Help says some support custom report types become available only when the feature is enabled. If the feature is intentionally off, I either enable it in a sandbox with a governance story or design a different type that does not need historical trending. I also confirm the user is looking in the correct report type category.
interview_questions.example: Sandbox without historical trending enabled; the Cases with Historical Trending type is absent.
tradeoffs: Enable a feature vs a simpler CRT
follow_ups: Name another feature-gated support CRT from Help.
Is this the same as a joined report block?
weak_answer_warnings: Inventing a license name not in Help

interview_questions.question: When would you avoid a custom report type even though a field is hard to report on?
interview_questions.answer_30_seconds: When the need is a different format, a filter/cross filter, a dashboard, or CRM Analytics/Tableau—not a missing object graph on the type.
interview_questions.answer_2_minutes: Custom report types solve missing objects and relationships. They do not replace summary versus matrix layout, row-level formulas, dynamic dashboards, or dataset recipes. If the field is on the type but users want buckets, that is ANA-003. If they want each rep to see their own numbers on a dashboard, that is running user (ANA-004). If they need multi-cloud joins and SAQL, that is CRM Analytics orientation (ANA-006). Creating extra CRTs also burns allocation.
interview_questions.example: Request is 'color-code deal size Small/Medium/Large'—bucketing, not a new CRT.
follow_ups: Where does a joined report fit?
What allocation applies in Developer Edition?

interview_questions.question: Teach custom report types without calling them a catalog or a filing cabinet.
interview_questions.answer_30_seconds: I use a tasting menu: the menu lists which courses can be ordered together. Must-have related records dumps anyone who skipped a course; with-or-without keeps them. The menu is metadata; tonight's plates are data.
interview_questions.answer_2_minutes: Standard menus are printed by Salesforce. Custom tasting menus are designed in Setup when a custom object is missing from the house menu. I show that a page layout is the plate presentation on a record page, not the menu. I state where the analogy breaks: Salesforce still applies FLS and sharing, and editions cap how many custom menus you may write. I finish with allocations from Help so the picture is not purely metaphorical.
interview_questions.example: Walk a sales manager through LAB_Account with optional site visits using the tasting-menu mapping.
follow_ups: Where does the tasting-menu analogy break?
Quote one official Help sentence about report types.
weak_answer_warnings: Falling back to a generic filing-cabinet story
